stem: Which home-safety teaching is appropriate for an older adult at risk for falls?

options.A: Limit routine walking inside the home so the older adult has fewer opportunities to experience a fall.
options.B: Remove tripping hazards, improve lighting, and install bathroom grab bars or other appropriate home-safety supports.
options.C: Keep familiar throw rugs in walking paths while adding brighter lighting to improve visual contrast.
options.D: Use loose backless slippers indoors because they are easier to remove if balance is lost.

rationale: Current CDC older-adult fall-prevention guidance recommends making the home safer by removing things that can be tripped over, improving lighting, installing grab bars in and around the tub or shower and next to the toilet, and adding stair railings. CDC also encourages strength and balance activity rather than unnecessary restriction of routine movement. Therefore B is correct. A promotes avoidable inactivity, C leaves a known tripping hazard in place, and D uses insecure footwear that can worsen fall risk.
educational_objective: Reduce home fall risk in older adults by removing trip hazards, improving lighting, installing grab bars/railings as needed, and supporting safe activity rather than environmental hazards or unnecessary immobility.
source_organization: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)
source_document_title: Preventing Falls and Hip Fractures; Information for Older Adults
source_version_date: Preventing Falls and Hip Fractures updated January 27, 2026; current CDC fall-prevention guidance live-rechecked August 16, 2026
source_locator: Preventing a fall or hip fracture > Make your home safer: get rid of trip hazards, add bathroom grab bars, railings on both sides of stairs, improve lighting. Strength and balance exercises are also recommended. Information for Older Adults explicitly identifies throw rugs as trip hazards and recommends brighter lighting and bathroom grab bars.
source_claim_supported: Older-adult home fall prevention includes removing trip hazards such as throw rugs/clutter, improving lighting and installing bathroom grab bars/other supports; routine safe mobility should not be restricted solely to reduce opportunities to fall.

correction_summary: Retained the home-fall-prevention construct and key B. Updated currentness to the January 2026 CDC page and strengthened the rationale by contrasting environmental hazard reduction with unnecessary mobility restriction and unsafe footwear.

audit_findings.source_authority: Current CDC fall-prevention guidance; NCSBN 2026 blueprint
audit_findings.currentness: CDC fall-prevention page updated 2026-01-27 and live-rechecked 2026-08-16
audit_findings.exact_locator: CDC Preventing Falls and Hip Fractures > Make your home safer and strength/balance sections; Information for Older Adults home-safety section
audit_findings.claim_audit: Final item uses direct CDC home-safety recommendations and avoids implying that reducing activity is an evidence-based substitute for hazard reduction and mobility support.

distractor_audit.A: Incorrect because safe activity/strength/balance is encouraged; unnecessary immobility can worsen function.
distractor_audit.C: Incorrect because throw rugs are recognized trip hazards that should be removed/secured rather than retained in walking paths.
distractor_audit.D: Incorrect because loose backless footwear can impair stability; CDC fall guidance favors addressing foot/footwear risk.

audit_findings.ambiguity_second_answer: Only B contains the CDC-recommended environmental fall-prevention measures without preserving or adding hazards.
audit_findings.cueing: All options are home-safety teaching strategies for the same older adult.
audit_findings.blueprint: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control — fall-risk reduction and environmental safety.
audit_findings.independent_second_pass: Rechecked current January 2026 CDC fall-prevention recommendations, all alternatives, rationale, objective, ambiguity, cueing and NCSBN category alignment. B remained uniquely correct.
